name: Hughes procedure

card.summary: A two-stage eyelid surgery that rebuilds a missing lower eyelid with a flap from the upper lid, restoring both the eyelid's function and a natural-looking eye contour.
card.note: A reconstructive operation for large lower-lid defects, usually after tumour removal; the eye is covered for weeks between stages.

quick.overview:
The Hughes procedure is an oculoplastic operation for rebuilding the back layer of a lower eyelid when a large part of it is missing, most often after a skin cancer is removed. A flap of tarsus and conjunctiva from the upper lid is advanced down to fill the gap and is covered at the front with skin or a graft, so the lid regains a normal edge, support and appearance.

It has been in use since Wendell Hughes described it in 1937 and remains a standard technique. Case series report good function and cosmetic results in most patients, with a minority needing a touch-up operation.
quick.how: It is carried out by an eye-plastic surgeon in two stages. In the first, the flap is attached to the lower-lid defect and the eyes stay joined for a period. In the second, several weeks later, the bridge is divided and the lid margin is shaped. Variants add grafts or other flaps for larger or corner-of-the-eye defects.
quick.risks: Reported complications include a lowered or notched lid margin, thinning of the lid, swelling, lashes or fine hairs rubbing the cornea, corneal surface problems, upper-lid retraction and entropion or ectropion. Vision in the operated eye is limited while the lids are joined, which is the main reason newer one-stage options are used when suitable.

lead: The Hughes procedure, or Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap, reconstructs the posterior layer of the lower eyelid using tissue taken from the upper lid [1][2]. It was first described in 1937 and is used chiefly for full-thickness defects in the central lower lid [2].

Its goal is to restore function, comfort and cosmesis together: a lid that closes, protects the eye and looks like the opposite side [3][4]. The anterior layer is rebuilt with a skin graft or flap, and surgeons have developed modifications that reduce donor-site and recipient-site problems [2].

The operation is mainly performed after removal of eyelid cancers such as basal cell carcinoma [3][5]. It is a reconstructive rather than elective cosmetic procedure; the wiki records it because it is a named eyelid surgery in appearance-related discussions.

chain: Upper-lid flap supplies the missing lower-lid back layer
Skin graft or flap restores the front layer
Lower lid regains normal position, edge and shape
angle.text: The procedure rebuilds a missing lower eyelid so the eye contour looks normal again after tumour removal or injury. People discuss it as an example of eyelid reconstruction aiming at both function and appearance.

infobox: Large lower-lid defects, often after tumour excision [3][5]

paras: A tarsoconjunctival flap from the upper eyelid is advanced into the lower-lid defect to replace the back layer, then covered in front with a skin graft or local flap [3][4]. Because the flap stays attached to the upper lid, the eyelids remain closed together after the first stage, and a second operation divides the flap a number of weeks later [1][5]. The bipedicle flap is a variant that keeps its blood supply through two tubed pedicles of conjunctiva and Mueller's muscle instead of a conjunctival apron [6].

A 1999 review outlines modifications over 60 years that reduced donor-site morbidity and improved results [2]. Variants include a maximal Hughes procedure with periosteal flaps for the largest defects, and a reverse modified technique that uses a lower-lid flap to rebuild the upper lid [7][8].

In a Salzburg series of 55 patients, 42 had good eyelid function and cosmesis; some needed secondary surgery or further treatment, and one had a major complication [9]. A series of 45 patients with large defects, many extending into the canthus, studied a Hughes flap with skin graft [10]. A 1988 description calls the technique's cosmetic and functional results outstanding while noting the drawback of keeping the lid closed for 2 to 8 weeks [5].

A 1992 review lists lowered lid margin, thinning, lymphoedema of the flap, margin defects, wound dehiscence, corneal epithelial defects, trichiasis from fine hairs, keratinisation of the margin, conjunctival ectropion, and upper-lid retraction or entropion [1].

A 2017 review notes the modified Hughes procedure is favourable for large defects but needs temporary eye closure, and describes single-stage alternatives such as the Smith-modified Kuhnt-Szymanowski procedure and flaps, along with cartilage grafts from the nose septum or ear for the back layer [11].

Published human studies are mostly retrospective case series of patients, largely older adults after tumour excision. The Salzburg series of 55 patients reported function and cosmesis restored in 42 [9], and a series of 45 patients with canthal involvement reported outcomes after division [10]. Other series report outcomes for the modified procedure after malignant tumour removal [12]. No randomised comparisons have been published.

timeline.event: Review of the flap's evolution over six decades [2].
Review discusses avoiding the Hughes flap in favour of one-stage options when suitable [11].
